progression.prerequisiteKnowledge: From b01: gene, allele and gene pool at three levels; a new allele starts as one copy; gene flow named ("when organisms or their pollen move between populations"); "selection and chance change how common they are". From B11: allele frequency by counting copies, two per individual for an autosomal gene, written as a decimal. From b07: mutation is the ultimate source of new alleles; meiosis and fertilisation reshuffle existing ones; alleles lost from a population are not made again without mutation. From b05: only germ-line mutations are inherited. Year 11: natural selection and selection pressure. Not assumed: genetic drift, sampling error, bottleneck, founder effect, gene flow as a force on frequency, evaluating relative effects.
progression.startsWith: Compare two population gene pools. The video opens: By the early 1990s, only about twenty to thirty Florida panthers were left, cut off in the swamps of southern Florida.
progression.stopsAfter: calculating an allele frequency as copies over total copies; explaining genetic drift as random sampling of alleles each generation, and why it changes frequencies more in small populations, including losing or fixing alleles regardless of their effect; describing a bottleneck and the founder effect as drift from a small random sample; explaining that mutation adds a new allele as a single copy (1 in 2N), so it changes a gene pool slowly and new alleles are often lost by drift in small populations; explaining gene flow as alleles moving with breeding migrants, which adds alleles a population lacked, changes frequencies quickly and makes populations more alike, without creating alleles; contrasting drift (random) with selection (non-random); evaluating which process matters most from population size, isolation and timescale, using the Florida panther case; applying this to an unseen allele-frequency calculation after a cyclone and an unseen conservation plan.
progression.nextLesson: what counts as biotechnology, from bread and selective breeding to modern techniques (route entry bio-m6-b09).

teaching.task: One species, two very different gene pools: what changes the alleles of a population, and which change matters most?
teaching.causalExplanation: Causes: why a frequency changes with no advantage (each generation is a random sample, 3); why small populations drift more (a small sample strays further, 3); why a crash or a few founders change frequencies (few individuals carry only a sample, 4); why harmful traits showed in the panthers (so few animals that relatives often bred together, 4); why mutation is slow (one copy in 2N, rare per gene, often lost, 5); why gene flow helped (it brought back lost alleles, so kittens had more genetic variation and fewer inbreeding signs, 6); why the judgement depends on context (size, isolation, time, 7). Visible case: one species, two basins, one rescue; every process acts on the same board. Video advantage: rings scooped into new basins, drift lines wandering, migrants carrying rings across. Thinking opportunities: two unseen items with every given on screen. Reading load: two basins and at most about three tags; the attempt cards are the densest frames and are the task.
teaching.conversationalApproach: The Florida panther and the Texas puma, one species with two very different gene pools, set the question of what changes a gene pool; the gene pool and allele frequency are recalled with one count; genetic drift is shown as chance sampling (only some animals breed, each parent passes on one allele of each pair by chance) with a coin and simulated populations, so size matters; bottleneck and founder effect follow as drift from a small sample; mutation adds one new copy, slowly; gene flow brings alleles in with moving, breeding animals and makes populations more alike; which process matters most is judged for a given population, with selection named as the non-random contrast. Two exam questions follow with brief feedback, then the decision rule hands off to biotechnology (b09).
teaching.openingDecision: By the early 1990s, only about twenty to thirty Florida panthers were left, cut off in the swamps of southern Florida. Many had kinked tails and poor-quality sperm, and some had heart defects. In Texas, pumas of the same species were doing fine. So in 1995, biologists released eight female Texas pumas into Florida. Within about a decade, the panther population had roughly tripled. What had gone wrong with the Florida panthers' alleles, and how did eight newcomers help fix it?
teaching.understandingCheck: 9a is a calculation and identify item: an island population of 500 skinks with allele b at frequency 0.1; a cyclone leaves 10 survivors, survival unrelated to this gene; the survivors carry 4 copies of b; calculate the new frequency (4 / 20 = 0.2), identify the process and justify. It tests copy counting (two per skink), the bottleneck as drift and the "random with respect to the gene" condition. 9c is an evaluate item on a hypothetical conservation plan: a small isolated population of 30 possums has lost much of its genetic variation; bring in 10 possums from a large population of the same species, or stay isolated and rely on mutation. It tests gene flow against mutation in a small population, with drift acting on both, and needs a verdict. Neither is the panther. Each ends "Pause here to answer." with a 10 s countdown; the full card stays on screen during and after the countdown. Each feedback is brief (about 25 to 30 s): answer, key reason, short working where needed, the givens underlined in the question strip as they are used, one crossed-out classic mistake. No givens card.
teaching.curriculumScope: "evaluate the effect of mutation, gene flow and genetic drift on the gene pool of populations (ACSBL091, ACSBL092)". The verb is "evaluate", so scene 7 makes a judgement by context, attempt 2 asks for one, and both model answers end with a verdict (bank trap: "Evaluate" needs a verdict). Inquiry question: "How does mutation introduce new alleles into a population?" Update the ledger row for B6-IQ1-06 when this design passes review.

design.visualSystem: One gene pool board throughout, built on b01's parts: each population is b01's `PoolBasin` (a rounded tray) holding b01's `AlleleRing` markers, one ring per allele copy (open ring "allele A", filled grey ring "allele a"; b01's amber notched ring `kind: 'new'` only for a new mutation; b01's `kind: 'flow'` ring, an open ring with a small blue arrow notch, for alleles that arrived by gene flow). Rings are never colour only (each kind has a shape mark). A coded frequency bar under each basin (b01's `FillBar`) shows the share of one allele, with the computed decimal on the word that says it. Two basins side by side carry the hook's comparison: "Texas" (large, many rings, varied) and "Florida" (small, few rings, two kinds missing). A drift strip (scene 3) draws simulated frequency lines across generations (computed by a seeded binomial sampler at N = 20 and N = 500, five replicates each, as the site's simulator; no axis numbers except "0", "0.5", "1"). Real animals are painted: the Florida panther and the Texas puma (new plates), placed above their basins; small population counts use the same plate at icon size in a grid (b01's `popGrid`), never people. Clutter rule (owner, 19 Oct): at most about three bright text items at once besides ring markers; each tag fades when the next cue lands.
design.transitionPlan: The map outline opens the hook and fades to the two pool basins with their plates; the top chips fill one per process as the board moves from the counted basin to the drift strip's simulated lines, the bottleneck scoop, one new amber ring and arriving flow rings; the JudgeTable fills one row per cue; memory lines write on beside their icons; each attempt clears the board and its feedback shrinks the card to a strip and builds the working and model answer one point at a time; the step chips and next chip close; scene crossfade with settle.
